rationale: B wins by a hair because its fourth angle, “Mercury says it's profitable on 200,000 businesses. Consumer banking will test that claim,” turns the thin launch facts into a real economics-scrutiny story without pretending pricing exists. A is strong, but “A business-first fintech goes consumer: is the 200,000-company base the distribution play?” leans on an unproven distribution thesis that has to be confirmed before it is a story. Both sets see the proof holes; B makes the sharpest hole one of the angles, which is usually where the coverage is hiding.
gaps_in_A: “the founders and employees who already bank at those 200,000 companies” is an inferred distribution story. The update says Mercury serves businesses, not that employees or founders are invite targets.
“What the SVB windfall became” overstates the fact pattern. The update says Mercury became well known after SVB, not that it got a measurable windfall.
“category-creation” and “Ladder lens” are insider scaffolding. Useful to the strategist, useless to a reporter.
It buries the economics tension. “The company says it is profitable” plus undisclosed pricing and deposit targets is a sharper kept angle than just another expansion frame.
gaps_in_B: “Mercury wants to hold consumers' money without being a bank” is punchy but sloppy. The update says partner banks provide banking services; the custody language needs precision.
“crisis-era winner converting its moment into a bigger ambition” overclaims causality. The supplied facts support reputation after SVB, not a proven conversion engine.
“from B2B (sophisticated customers) to individuals” adds an unsupported judgment about customer sophistication.
The next step is too generic. Before “resolve the shape into a real named reporter,” Mercury needs partner-bank names, FDIC mechanics, and profitability substantiation in hand.
